# The model is not the product

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-model-is-not-the-product/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-03 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Buyers do not pay for a model. They pay for a finished job. Position on the job, prove every AI claim, and tell investors a different story from customers. The market has made this sharper: 37% of enterprises in a16z's 2025 CIO survey used five or more models, and model market share swings by double digits in a year, so a pitch built on the model is a pitch any competitor can copy.

## Key points

- The model is shared infrastructure; enterprises now buy from several model providers at once and switch by use case.
- Positioning starts where the model ends: the closed ticket, the reconciled ledger, the redlined contract, named in the buyer's words.
- Answer the wrapper objection by showing you own data, distribution or workflow depth, with proof. One is enough to start; two is a business.
- Unsupported AI claims are now an enforcement matter: the FTC and SEC have both acted against companies that overstated what their AI did.
- Investors buy the category; customers buy this task, this team, this cost and this quarter. Write them as separate documents on one claims register.

## Why every pitch sounds the same

The model is shared infrastructure. Whatever it can do today, your competitor's version can do by Tuesday. So pitches that lead with the model converge. "AI-powered." "Built on frontier models." "Intelligent assistant for X." The buyer cannot tell you apart and stops trying.

The buyer data shows why. Andreessen Horowitz's 2025 survey of 100 enterprise CIOs found 37% used five or more models, up from 29% a year earlier, choosing by use case rather than loyalty. One leader told the researchers that "for most tasks, all the models perform well enough now." Menlo Ventures' 2026 survey shows how quickly the supply side moves: Google's share of enterprise model API spend fell from 21% to 9% in a year, while Anthropic's rose from 40% to 55%. If your advantage is the model you picked, it is an advantage you rent, and the lease is short.

Positioning starts where the model ends. What does the buyer have at the end that they did not have before? A closed ticket. A reconciled ledger. A contract redlined to their playbook. Name that, in the buyer's words, and the model becomes a detail.

## Workflow and outcome over model

Write your one product truth ([Part 2](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/)) without naming a model, a vendor or the word AI. If you cannot, you have described a feature, not a product.

Then map the workflow. Where does the work start? Who touches it? What breaks today? Where does your product sit, and what does it hand back?

Most of the value in AI products lives in the unglamorous parts. Intake. Retrieval. Permissions. Review. Exceptions. The hand-off to the system of record. That is also where it gets hard to copy. A competitor can match your prompt in an afternoon. Matching your exception handling takes a year of customer calls.

The same a16z survey adds a commercial reason to invest there. It found that agentic workflows were making it harder for enterprises to switch between models, because the prompts, tools and checks around each model become tuned to it. The switching cost sits in the workflow. A vendor that owns the workflow owns the switching cost; a vendor that only resells the model does not.

## The wrapper objection

You will hear "isn't this just a wrapper?" from investors, buyers and engineers. Do not argue. Agree that the model is rented, then show which of three things you own.

| What you own | What it looks like | How to prove it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data | Proprietary, labelled or permissioned data the model cannot see | Show results with and without it |
| Distribution | A channel, install base or integration the model provider does not have | Show where the users come from |
| Workflow depth | The steps around the prompt that make it fit a real job | Show a user doing the job end to end |

One is enough to start. Two is a business. If you own none, the objection stands, and polishing the deck will not fix it.

Distribution deserves more weight than most founders give it. Our analysis of [why AI companies have a distribution problem disguised as a model problem](https://lowob.com/research/ai-companies-distribution-problem/) sets out the evidence that buyers now choose on fit, proof and integration. If your answer to the wrapper question is "distribution", the proof is a chart of where users came from and what it cost to reach them.

> A competitor can match your prompt in an afternoon. Matching your exception handling takes a year of customer calls.

## AI claims in the claims register

AI products attract claims that cannot survive a demo. Put every one in the register from [Part 2](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/), with evidence, owner and date.

This is no longer only a matter of buyer trust. In September 2024 the US Federal Trade Commission announced Operation AI Comply, including action against a company that marketed itself as "the world's first robot lawyer" without testing its output against lawyers' work; the chair said there was "no AI exemption from the laws on the books." In March 2024 the SEC settled charges against two investment advisers for claiming AI capabilities they did not have, which the SEC chair called "AI washing." Gartner estimated in 2025 that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors marketing agentic AI were real, the practice our explainer on [agent washing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-washing/) covers.

| Claim | The question it must answer | Evidence that holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accuracy | On what dataset, measured how, by whom, when? | A dated eval on a described test set, demo and production numbers labelled separately |
| "Agent" | Does it act without a human in the loop, for which steps, and what happens when it is wrong? | A list of actions it takes alone and those that need approval |
| "Learns from your data" | Does the model update, or does retrieval? | A plain statement of which, and where customer data goes |
| Time or cost saved | Against what baseline, for which task? | A before and after on one named workflow |

Accuracy: production accuracy is lower than demo accuracy. Say which one you are quoting. If you only have the demo number, say that too. Our explainer on [AI evals](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/) covers how to build a test a buyer can read.

"Agent": if a human approves every action, call it an assistant. Buyers trust you more for it, and the security review goes faster. Our explainer on [AI autonomy levels](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-autonomy-level/) gives a vocabulary for saying exactly how much the product does alone.

"Learns from your data": they are different products with different risks. Say which.

Anything without a test behind it comes out of the copy. Not softened. Out.

## Investor story and customer story

Investors buy the category. Why this workflow, why now, why you will own the data or the distribution in three years.

Customers buy Tuesday. This task, this team, this cost, this risk, this quarter.

Mixing them hurts both. Customers hear "platform" and wait for the roadmap. Investors hear a feature list and see a tool. Write both stories, keep them in separate documents, and make sure the same claims register underwrites each one. If a claim is only in the investor deck, ask why. The SEC case above involved claims made to clients in filings and marketing; a claim that would embarrass you in a customer's procurement file should not be in an investor deck either. Our piece on [raising for an AI company](https://lowob.com/research/raising-for-an-ai-company/) covers what investors now test.

## The checklist

| Check | Done when |
| --- | --- |
| Product truth | Written without "AI", a model name or a vendor name |
| Workflow map | End to end, with your product's entry and exit points marked |
| Wrapper answer | Data, distribution or workflow depth, with proof |
| Claims register | Every accuracy and "agent" claim has a test behind it |
| Two stories | Investor story and customer story in separate documents |
| Homepage test | Still makes sense with "AI" deleted |

## lowob takeaways

- **Write the product truth without the model.** No model name, no vendor name, no "AI".
- **Own something the model provider does not.** Data, distribution or workflow depth, with proof.
- **Treat AI claims as testable statements.** Regulators already do.
- **Keep two stories on one register.** Investors buy the category; customers buy this task, team, cost and risk this quarter.

## Common questions

### How should an AI startup position its product?

Position on the finished job, in the buyer's words, not on the model. Map the workflow end to end and show where your product sits and what it hands back. Enterprises use several models and switch by use case, so the model is not a durable point of difference.

### How do I answer the "it's just a wrapper" objection?

Agree the model is rented, then show which of three things you own: proprietary data, distribution, or workflow depth, with proof. One is enough to start; two is a business.

### When should an AI product be called an agent?

Only if it acts without a human in the loop, and you should say for which steps and what happens when it is wrong. If a human approves every action, call it an assistant. Gartner estimated only about 130 vendors marketing agentic AI were genuine.

### Can an AI company get in trouble for exaggerating what its AI does?

Yes. The FTC's Operation AI Comply and the SEC's 2024 "AI washing" settlements both targeted companies whose AI claims were not supported. Every claim should have a test, an owner and a date behind it.
